bib.title: Chapter 4. Deep Q-Networks (in Reinforcement Learning: Industrial Applications of Intelligent Agents)

question: How can Q-learning be scaled from lookup tables to large or continuous state spaces using neural-network function approximators, and what do DQN and its extensions (Rainbow and others) cost and buy in practice?
contributions: Reviews neural network architectures and frameworks as context for deep RL
Explains DQN: experience replay, Q-network clones (target network), network architecture and loss
Worked example comparing random, tabular Q-learning and DQN agents on CartPole using Intel Coach
Case study of NFQ in a smart thermostat (Marantos et al.)
Rainbow DQN components: distributional RL (C51), prioritized replay, noisy nets, dueling networks
Worked example training DQN and Rainbow on Atari Pong and Ms Pac-Man with time and cost figures
Other DQN improvements: exploration (bootstrapped DQN, ensembles), quantile regression, learning from offline data (BCQ)

results.claim: Training the DQN agent on Atari took on average 4.8 hours and about $5.80 per million frames in Coach on a GCP P4 GPU VM.
results.setup: Coach Atari presets, default hyperparameters, GCP n1-standard-4 VM with one Nvidia Tesla P4 GPU, games Pong and Ms Pac-Man, one run each
results.quote: The DQN agent, on average, takes 4.8 hours and costs $5.80 to train upon one
results.note: Table 4-1 lists DQN Pong 2M frames 10 h $12 and Ms. Pac-Man 3M frames 14 h $17; the per-million figures in the text are averages of these, not table cells.

results.claim: Rainbow took on average 7.6 hours and about $8.50 per million frames, nearly double DQN's cost.
results.setup: Same as DQN: Coach presets with default (different) hyperparameters per agent, GCP P4
results.quote: The Rainbow agent takes 7.6 hours and costs $8.50 to
results.note: Table 4-1: Rainbow Pong 2.5M frames 19 h $22; Ms. Pac-Man 3M frames 23 h $26. Author says values are indicators, affected by differing hyperparameters.

results.claim: On CartPole a random policy averages about 25 steps, because that is how long the pole takes to fall.
results.setup: CartPole (OpenAI Gym), reward 1 per step, random agent implemented in Coach
results.quote: able to achieve an average reward of approximately 25 steps.
results.note: Read from Figure 4-1, which is not averaged and noisy; no run count given.

results.claim: Tabular Q-learning matched DQN on CartPole only after feature engineering that left about 150 discrete states.
results.setup: CartPole, observation states multiplied by 10, rounded to integer, only pole angle and angular velocity used; DQN used raw inputs unchanged
results.quote: This results in approximately 150 states in the Q-value lookup
results.where: CartPole example; 'Which is better? DQN versus Q-learning'

results.claim: Rainbow needed about 0.5 million more frames than DQN to reach a similar Pong result, which the author attributes possibly to different hyperparameters.
results.metric: extra frames to similar Pong reward
results.setup: Pong, Coach presets; DQN epsilon-greedy vs Rainbow parameter-noise exploration; Rainbow learning rate 6.25e-5
results.quote: The Rainbow agent takes an extra 0.5 million frames to obtain a similar result
results.note: Table 4-1 gives DQN 2M and Rainbow 2.5M frames for Pong. Author's claim that Rainbow would match DQN with similar hyperparameters is a prediction, not measured.

results.claim: In a cited thermostat study, an NFQ agent cut average energy use by up to 59% against a threshold-based thermostat.
results.source: Marantos et al. 2018, Towards Plug&Play Smart Thermostats Inspired by Reinforcement Learning
results.setup: Simulation of a real building in Crete, Greece with public weather data; depends on comfort level chosen; agent ran on a Raspberry Pi Zero
results.quote: age energy usage by up to 59%, depending on the level of comfort chosen.
results.where: Case Study: Reducing Energy Usage in Buildings

results.claim: A DQN agent trained only on another DQN agent's replay buffer on CartPole performed poorly with diverging Q-values, while a BCQ agent on the same buffer converged with stable Q-values.
results.setup: CartPole in Coach; buffer generated by a standard DQN agent; second agent never explores; shown in Fig 4-13 (reward and mean Q-values on log y-axis); no numbers printed
results.note: Qualitative, read from a figure; single experiment, no seeds stated.

results.claim: CartPole is solved at an average reward of at least 195 over 100 consecutive trials; episodes cap at 200 steps and both Q-learning and DQN reach the cap.
results.setup: CartPole (OpenAI Gym), episode ends at pole angle beyond 12 degrees, cart position beyond 2.4, or length over 200 steps
results.quote: average reward greater than or equal to 195 over 100

results.claim: C51 predicts a 51-bin histogram of returns trained as classification with cross-entropy loss.
results.source: Bellemare et al. 2017, A Distributional Perspective on Reinforcement Learning
results.setup: Distributional RL description; author says performance is proportional to bin count with diminishing returns

limits: Atari results are two games, one run each, with default Coach hyperparameters that differ between DQN and Rainbow, so the author says no firm conclusions can be drawn from single episodes.
Training stopped early (about 2 to 3 million frames); the author predicts convergence at 20 million frames but leaves it as a reader exercise.
No reward numbers for the Atari or CartPole runs are printed; results are in figures only.
DQN versus Rainbow cost comparison is called an indicator only, affected by differing hyperparameters.
Chapter predates 2021; coverage of exploration and offline RL is a short survey of 2016-2019 work.
Experience replay buffer size is noted as a sensitivity (Zhang and Sutton) but not tuned in the chapter.
practices: Use an absolute (Huber) loss in noisy environments and a squared loss in simple, noise-free ones (CartPole example tip).
Choose a network architecture that fits the domain: CNN for images, RNN for time series, MLP for multisensor data (Deep Reinforcement Learning).
Use a randomly sampled experience replay buffer and a target network to make DQN stable (Experience Replay, Q-Network Clones).
Consider reward distributions, not just means, when working in stochastic environments (Ms Pac-Man discussion).
Start with a wrapper library such as Keras or Gluon, then graduate to PyTorch (Deep Learning Frameworks tip).
Weigh Rainbow's gain against its near doubling of compute before adopting it (Atari Results).
Use tabular Q-learning with engineered features if explainability and robustness in production matter more than convenience (DQN versus Q-learning).
Use online learning when the agent must explore; use standard ML if the problem is not sequential or needs no exploration (Why train online?).
For logged data without interaction, use batch-constrained methods such as BCQ rather than plain DQN (Learning from Offline Data).

terms.definition: a buffer of observations, actions, rewards, and subsequent observations that can be used to train the DL model; random subsets break the correlation between consecutive observations
agents forget experiences when observations drop off the end of a first in, first out buffer, leading to a large change in policy
a second network whose weights are copied periodically so the data the agent sees is stationary for a limited time
the agent converges but never stabilizes, oscillating
treating the return as a random variable and learning its distribution rather than its expectation
distributional agent using a discrete parametric distribution, a histogram of 51 bins, trained with cross-entropy
samples the replay buffer with probability proportional to the absolute error of the temporal-difference update
augmenting epsilon-greedy search by adding noise in the neural network
individual actions represented relative to the state-value average
a single NN with two heads, one estimating the state-value function and the other the advantage function, recombined into the action-value function
the task of learning a policy from a fixed dataset without further interaction from the environment
batch-constrained deep Q-learning: a conditional variational autoencoder generates only actions leading to states in the buffer, with two Q-networks clipped for low-variance updates
reusing a randomly selected policy to drive exploration deeper into unobserved states, as in bootstrapped DQN
